title: Pickthall and the 1934 translation
hook: two early English translations, both by Muslims, both still read

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arabic: the Qur'an as the Arabic itself, and a translation as its meanings. Your line was a translation is a meaning. Day three hundred twenty.

All year, when this path has quoted the Qur'an in English, you've heard one particular voice. Thee and thou. Lo! Verily. "But lo! with hardship goeth ease." That's Marmaduke Pickthall, an Englishman whose translation was published in 1930. Why him? Partly because his translation is old enough to be free for anyone to quote. But it's also one of two early English translations, both by Muslims, that people still read nearly a century later.
screen: `THEE, THOU, LO, VERILY.` → `AN ENGLISHMAN, PUBLISHED 1930.` → `TWO EARLY TRANSLATIONS.`

segments.voice: Pickthall was the son of an English country clergyman. He became a novelist, traveled in Syria, Palestine and Turkey, and grew to love the Muslim world he met there. In London, during the First World War, he publicly declared himself a Muslim. Later he went to India and worked in the service of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who gave him leave to finish his translation. Before publishing, he took it to Cairo to go over it with scholars there. It appeared in 1930 as The Meaning of the Glorious Koran. He aimed to be almost literal, close to the Arabic's order, in the solemn English of the old Bible that his readers would recognize as scripture. That's why it can feel stiff, and also why it can feel like thunder. The second came from an Indian Muslim scholar who had served in the civil service in India, and began appearing in 1934. Its English flows more, with a rhythm close to poetry, and it carries long explanatory notes, like reading with a teacher at your shoulder. Later publishers revised some of those notes, so editions differ, and readers check which one they hold. Two Muslims, two temperaments: one stays close to the Arabic's shape and lets you do the work; one opens the meaning out and explains as it goes. That's the gift of reading more than one. Where they agree, you're probably close to the meaning. Where they differ, you've found a place where the Arabic holds more than one English sentence can carry.
screen: `AN ENGLISH NOVELIST BECOMES MUSLIM` · `ALMOST LITERAL, IN OLD ENGLISH` · `A SECOND VOICE, FROM 1934` · `WHERE THEY DIFFER, LOOK CLOSER`

segments.voice: Say Pickthall's line from Surah 94 slowly, twice, and hear the old English, goeth, not goes: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease." Stay with the word with: not after hardship, but with it. If something is hard for you right now, set it beside that word, and let the line sit there.
Pickthall. The English convert whose 1930 translation, close to the Arabic and solemn as scripture, this path has quoted all year.
Your line: two voices, one line. Each one catches something the other leaves out. That's day three hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Many English-speaking Muslims read the Qur'an's meanings in more than one translation, often Pickthall's 1930 rendering alongside the 1934 translation and newer ones, usually printed beside the Arabic.

Pickthall biography (born 1875; son of a clergyman; declared Islam 1917 in London; Hyderabad; consulted scholars in Cairo, 1929; published 1930): confirm.
The 1934 translator: Indian Civil Service; first parts published in Lahore from 1934; about 6,000 notes; later revised editions (e.g. 1980s). Confirm.
'Among the most widely printed English Qur'ans' is a general claim; confirm or soften.
